tagline: Extending Király and Tokai's dictionary of the Rohonc Codex
intro:
The Rohonc Codex is a small paper book of the sixteenth century. It is kept at the Library of the Hungarian Academy of Sciences in Budapest. It is written in a script that occurs in no other document. The script runs right to left and uses several hundred signs.

Levente Zoltán Király and Gábor Tokai established what the book contains. They published a dictionary of 841 signs and the grammar. The book contains the apocryphal Life of Adam and Eve running into the legend of the Rood. It contains the story of Joachim and Anne. It contains a Passion the codex itself says it takes from Matthew and John. It contains sermons and parables for the gospels of the year. It contains the Finding of the Cross. It contains the Acts of the Apostles. At the end are a few pages of one man's diary. The frame is a revelation. An angel of God speaks and the prophet Elijah is the one addressed.

This project started from Király and Tokai's dictionary. It tested their dictionary and extended it. It read signs their dictionary leaves undefined. It checked every reading at every place the sign stands in the book. It rendered the whole manuscript into English. Every word is marked by how well it is known.
how_far: The manuscript contains 29,997 words. This project reads 93.4 percent of them. 3.2 percent are read from one passage only. 3.3 percent are restored in brackets. 0.2 percent are dark. 81.6 percent of lines have every word read. Lines are complete once brackets are counted 98.9 percent of the time.
tiers: The dictionary of added readings has 1,787 entries. They are graded by how well they are known. Tier A readings survive every place the sign stands in the book. Tier B readings survive most places. Tier C and D readings are read from one passage with nothing inside the book able to refuse them. Tier G is a guess printed in brackets and counted as read nowhere. Withdrawn readings stay in the file with the reason they went.

dictionary_lead:
This dictionary lists the readings this project added to Király and Tokai's work. Their own 841 entries are not reproduced here. The signs are written as glyph codes. Each glyph is three hexadecimal digits. The drawn signs are on their site.

The dictionary is searchable by reading or sign. It can be filtered by tier. Each entry shows the evidence line. The evidence line lists the folios and lines where the sign stands.
data_lead: This page provides every file the site is built from. The files include the dictionary and folio English as JSON. They include the rendering and the reader's edition. They include every saved run and the outside readers' replies.
outside_lead: Two outside reviewers were shown the write-up and asked what tests they would require. The following specification is quoted from one reviewer.
script_intro:
The writing runs right to left. The codex dates itself 1593. It is logographic. A sign stands for a word or a whole phrase, not a sound. Király and Tokai established this. Several hundred signs are in use.

Where the signs came from is not settled. This project does not claim to know. The script occurs in no other document. What can be said is structural. A logographic script is not tied to any one language. A sign meaning Lord can be voiced in whatever the reader speaks. That is an argument from the structure of the script. It is not a tested result.
script_signs: The following shuffler shows one sign's reading at a time.
script_numerals: Numerals are strokes that add. A ten written after a group multiplies that group by ten. This was checked four times. Ten-ten-ten-ten is forty at the forty days and forty nights. Two-two-ten is also forty at the forty days of rain. Six-two is eight at the circumcision on the eighth day. Six-six is twelve at the twelve apostles.
script_phrases: Phrases are written without a space. The example Király and Tokai print is you-Mary. That is a single sign made of their sign for the second person pronoun joined to their sign for Mary.
script_marks: The marks in the rendering have these meanings. A plain word is read. A word with an asterisk was read from one passage with nothing in the book able to refuse it. A word in brackets is a restoration and is counted as read nowhere. A hyphen inside a word means one sign read as the smaller signs it is built from. A tilde marks a spelling their own apparatus files as a variant.
script_plates: Twenty-six folios carry pictures. There are forty-nine pictures in all. The plates in this edition were redrawn. They are new drawings made by an image model from the library's low-resolution scan. No print-quality scan is available. They follow the scribe's composition.
method_intro:
The method solves the problem of reading one unread sign. It starts from Király and Tokai's dictionary. The only outside evidence is the source passage their notes cite for most folios.

The method is checkable. It writes the evidence line for every reading into a file. Anyone can repeat the check or overturn it. The bar for every test is written into the test's own file before it runs. A near miss is a miss.
method_loop: The loop that reads one unread sign has six numbered steps.
method_bars: The bar for every test is written into the test's own file before it runs. It is never moved afterwards. A near miss is a miss. Failed attempts are kept. They are written up with the number they failed by.

tests_intro:
The tests check the project's own readings. They were designed to break those readings. The bar for each test is declared first. It is written into the test's own file before the test runs.

Two outside reviewers were shown the write-up. They were asked what tests they would require. Those tests were run as specified.
tests_after: The passes and failures add up to a picture of what the method can and cannot do.

The site uses several sources. Each source is the work of its named author or institution. The following sentences say what each citation is to this project.

Király and Tokai put their transcription online so their claims could be checked. Their own translation of the codex is unpublished. Nothing on this site is it.

tests_note: Two things are worth saying plainly. The passage map can be recovered from Király and Tokai's words alone. It does not depend on anything this project read. The two instruments an outside reviewer specified for the search itself gave no verdict either way. They do not model the search as it was run.
code_lead: The programs run on the published data. Each test states its bar in its own first lines. The repository itself is not public.
sources_not_here: Király and Tokai's dictionary is not on this site. Their transcription is not on this site. Their page records are not on this site. The library scans are not on this site. The one thing of theirs used is the shape of the signs. The shapes are drawn from the outlines in their font. The font file itself is never served. The shapes are the sixteenth-century scribe's.

method_steps.d: Take the folio's own citation. Király and Tokai's notes cite a chapter and verse for most folios. The source passage is the only outside evidence there is.
Look at every line where the unread sign stands. Do not look only at the one line in hand.
Guess from the passage. The guess is the word the verse supplies for that slot.
Check the guess at every other occurrence in the book. A reading that fits where it was found and fails elsewhere is thrown away. It is not softened.
Grade the reading. Tier A fits everywhere checked. Tier B fits most. Tier C or D was read from one passage with nothing able to refuse it. Tier G is a guess in brackets.
Write the evidence line into the proposals file. The line includes the folios and lines. Anyone can repeat the check or overturn it.

method_mistakes_list.t: Treating a sign as an atom
method_mistakes_list.d: Eleven attempts assumed one sign meant one word with a meaning to guess. Many signs are short phrases written without a space. Both halves were already in the dictionary. That was the whole game.
Asking whether Holy Word inherits meaning from Word gave a true negative that looked like a dead end. The right question was whether signs combine.
Figures were computed per glyph when a word averages 2.43 glyphs. Every number moved when it was fixed. Always confirm what one row of the transcription is before measuring it.
Keying a scraped dictionary by code and keeping the last entry made the book's commonest word read eleven when it is and. Sixty-five codes had to be merged.

A failed aligner was predicted to be failing because it used only the four gospels. 1.75 million words of the wider sources were fetched and it scored no better. Test the cheap version of a corpus hypothesis first.
Király and Tokai's entries carry variant spellings in their own apparatus. Keying by headword silently dropped 88 signs. That is 1.2 percent of the book that they had already read.

Three versions of the arithmetic of what is left to read were wrong. One counted a line as reached while an unread word still stood in it. The current figures are measured. The wrong ones are kept on the page beside them.
